 EDITORIAL: We’re Colorado, not California. NO on 87 & NN; YES on 136
 By The Gazette Editorial Board 
 Published November 1, 2026 5:00am 
 + 
 Add Denver Gazette on Google
 FILE PHOTO 
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 Colorado is at a crossroads — and even the national media have taken notice. A headline in The Wall Street Journal last week said it all: 
 “Big Tax-and-Spend Stakes in Colorado / A pair of ballot measures would begin to turn the state into California.”
 Recommended Stories
 ▶ 
 Colorado has become a hotbed of democracy innovation | Vince Bzdek
 Rural Coloradans have a chance to elect another ‘brand’ | Pius Kamau 
 Voters will ask, ‘About last night?’ | Jon Caldara
 The “pair” is Amendment 87 and Proposition NN on the Nov. 3 statewide ballot. Both would have a cataclysmic impact.
 Amendment 87 is a $2.7 billion tax hike — the largest in state history — masquerading as “tax reform.” It would cast off Colorado’s fair and simple flat tax and replace it with a complicated array of tax brackets that would penalize productivity and chase off prosperity.
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 Proposition NN is the legislature’s underhanded attempt to end taxpayers’ TABOR refunds for the foreseeable future. It would gut historic constitutional spending limits that have helped keep runaway government growth in check since 1992. NN would balloon the state budget to unprecedented proportions — by up to $5 billion a year.
 Both measures would bleed money out of the private sector that creates most of Colorado’s jobs. They would sap our state’s ability to compete for new business investment and job growth — losing both to states with lower or no income tax.
 In other words, Tuesday’s election will be crunch time for Colorado — and not just because of the hotly contested congressional races on the ballot that will help decide control of the U.S. House. More so than any of the candidates vying for office on Tuesday’s ballot, 87 and NN will have a deep and far-reaching impact on our state’s ability to thrive. 
 Meanwhile, another proposal on the ballot could be the saving grace. That’s Proposition 136, a counterpunch to 87 that would cap the state’s income tax at its current 4.4% rate; 136 will trump 87’s tax hike even if both measures pass — so long as 136 nets more votes.
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 The Gazette editorial board urges a “no” vote for 87 and NN. And it urges a “yes” vote for 136. 
 (Go to https://www.denvergazette.com/2026/10/26/denver-gazette-editorial-board-recommendations-nov-3-ballot/ for The Denver Gazette’s full slate of ballot recommendations.)
 Make no mistake, there is absolutely no need for all the extra tax dollars 87 and NN would pump into state government coffers. The revenue windfall won’t go to essential services like Colorado’s crumbling, neglected highways or to public safety — in a state with one of the highest overall crime levels in the country. 
 The money will go to growing government programs. It will further engorge the likes of Medicaid, which already consumes a third of the state budget because lawmakers expanded its coverage to include medical services many taxpayers don’t get in their own health plans.
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 And NN’s promise to funnel more funding to public schools ignores the unanswered question: What happened to the whopping 41% increase the legislature poured into K-12 spending over the past five years? That’s in a state with declining school enrollment.
 If both 87 and NN pass, that won’t be the end of the state’s money grab, either. 
 The Wall Street Journal predicts, “Don’t expect this new revenue to satisfy progressives and government unions. It won’t be long before they seek to hit taxpayers for more money, as they have in California, New York and New Jersey. Once states embark on this tax-and-spending ratchet, and especially without the limit of a flat tax, they don’t stop.”
 It’s a sobering call on Colorado to walk back from the cliff’s edge. At the cliff’s bottom lies a state that long ago sold its soul to taxing and spending — and many of its refugees have since come to Colorado. 
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 Let’s heed the warning.
 We’re Colorado, not California. Vote NO on 87 and NN, and YES on 136.
